newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: COUNCIL TALKS LIFT HOPES CZECH RAIL STRIKE WILL END.
newsitem.headline: COUNCIL TALKS LIFT HOPES CZECH RAIL STRIKE WILL END.

text.p: The Czech Union of Industry and Transport on Friday said it had called a special meeting with government officials and business leaders -- the so-called Tripartite Council -- in an attempt to end a nationwide rail strike.
The strike, which began last Sunday as a 48-hour work stoppage, was extended to a fourth day on Friday after both unions and the government dug in their heels, adopting hardline stances.
But Jaromir Dusek, head of the Czech Association of Railworkers' Unions (OSZ), said he was hopeful the Tripartite meeting could find room for the two sides to bring an end to the action.
"We certainly are optimistic that the extension of the strike (to Friday midnight) will be the last (extension)," he told the daily Mlada Fronta Dnes on Friday.

Unions, which called the strike on Sunday, are demanding the removal of Czech Railway's management and a total rethink of plans to reform the dilapidated rail system which could cost tens of thousands of jobs.
The tripartite meeting follows an appeal from President Vaclav Havel on Thursday for officials to end the country's rail strike.
However, Prime Minster Vaclav Klaus who espouses Thatcherite free-market policies while often showing a willingness to compromise in practice, continues to take a tough line against the strikers.
Klaus has called the union's methods "irresponsible" and its demands "unacceptable" saying he would not meet union leaders until the strike was called off.
Deputy Prime Minister Ivan Kocarnik was slated to be the highest ranking government official at the Tripartite meeting on Friday.
The strike is the first major confrontation between organised labour and the government since the fall of communism in 1989.
So far it has had little impact on daily life but businesses fear the shutdown in freight service will start to bite into earnings if the strike lasts longer.
Cities have added buses to relieve commmuter pressure, but international trains have been stranded at borders with Germany, Poland, Austria, and Slovakia.
